papers.title: Navigating Runtime Dynamism in Semantic Query Serving
papers.abstract: LLM-powered semantic queries increasingly combine relational processing with multiple LLM-based operators over unstructured data. Efficiently serving such queries is challenging due to runtime dynamism at two coupled levels. Across queries, dynamic arrivals and heterogeneous resource demands continuously change scheduling priorities. Within a query, heterogeneous characteristics across fine-grained input batches cause operator costs and selectivities to vary throughout execution, making a statically optimized plan unreliable. These two forms of dynamism create a circular dependency: inter-query scheduling requires estimates of remaining LLM work, while the remaining work depends on runtime plan choices whose costs become observable only during execution. We present SeqoFlow, a runtime framework that jointly adapts query plans and schedules concurrent semantic queries. SeqoFlow enumerates equivalence-preserving plan alternatives under operator dependencies and decomposes queries into fine-grained units, enabling safe plan adaptation and query preemption at batch boundaries. To support both decisions without exhaustively profiling candidate plans on the target LLM, SeqoFlow uses lightweight speculative estimation to capture runtime costs. These estimates jointly guide plan adaptation and inter-query scheduling, closing the loop between query optimization and LLM inference. Experiments across diverse query structures, data distributions, and arrival rates show that SeqoFlow substantially reduces end-to-end latency compared to existing semantic query systems, adaptive query processing techniques, and conventional scheduling policies.

papers.title: Text-to-SQL Models Make Choices Without Saying So
papers.abstract: A text-to-SQL answer can run, return a plausible number and still compute something other than what the analyst meant. This can happen when the request leaves a calculation choice open, such as whether to count rows or distinct entities, and the model settles it without saying so. Standard benchmarks cannot detect this, because they score each question against a single reference interpretation. We introduce SpecBridge, which tests such a choice by varying it alone: it poses three otherwise identical requests, one leaving the choice open and one per interpretation, and scores each answer by running it. The databases are real, and the choices are ones that made models fail on existing benchmarks. On 204 hand-validated tests, four language models usually compute each interpretation when asked for it, yet for the open request return both in only 15-58% of the tests where they can, often without mentioning the choice. The gap lies in reporting, not in computing. Benchmarks even penalize the alternative: on BIRD questions where such a choice changes the answer, over two in five of the answers marked wrong are right under the other interpretation. Because the gap lies in reporting, a system can narrow it without a stronger model: it first decides whether a request leaves a choice open, then answers each interpretation in its own call. On our tests and on AMBROSIA, an existing benchmark of ambiguous questions, this approach raises the share of open requests that get every interpretation by 29-63 points over the single answer that production assistants give, without lowering precision on clear requests. It also needs fewer user turns than asking a clarifying question.

papers.title: Order-Dependent Complexity of Enumeration and Direct Access for Conjunctive Queries on Dynamic Data
papers.abstract: This note studies the fine-grained complexity of ranked enumeration and ranked direct access of conjunctive query answers over a dynamic database. We focus on lexicographically sorted answers, defined by an ordering on the query's free variables. From the literature, when no particular order is required, we know that when the query is self-join-free and q-hierarchical, we can build a data structure for enumeration (resp. direct access) with linear (resp. linearithmic) preprocessing and constant (resp. logarithmic) update time in the size of the database. For enumeration (resp. direct access), this data structure yields an algorithm that enumerates all query answers (resp. that returns the $k$-th query answer) with constant delay (resp. logarithmic access time). Our goal is to extend these results to ranked enumeration and ranked direct access, with the ranking function defined by a lexicographic order. We define a property on the order over the variables of $Q$, which we call being hierarchy-consistent. Given a user-specified query and hierarchy-consistent order, we first propose, for ranked enumeration under updates, an algorithm with linear preprocessing and logarithmic update time that enumerates all the query answers according to the user-specified order with constant delay. Moreover, for ranked direct access under updates, we propose an algorithm with linear preprocessing and logarithmic update time that returns the $k$-th tuple according to the user-specified order with logarithmic access time. In contrast, given a user-specified query and non-hierarchy-consistent order, we show a lower bound for ranked direct access under updates.

papers.title: ZeroGR: Filtering-First Constrained Decoding for Generative Recommendation
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation is gaining traction in production, retrieving items by generating their identifiers one token at a time. The generated sequences must identify relevant catalog items, so constrained decoding couples relevance scoring with validity filtering. Because most possible sequences are invalid, scoring before filtering wastes computation on candidates that will be discarded. Our evaluation shows that filtering first can avoid this work with negligible impact on recommendation quality. We present ZeroGR, a filtering-first constrained decoding system for generative recommendation. ZeroGR uses a step-sliced filtering index to reduce GPU memory use by tailoring data representations to each decoding step. Its execution engine adopts shared-slot execution to accelerate data exchange across stages and hybrid projection to adapt computation to workload patterns, thereby reducing execution overhead. During index refreshes, ZeroGR applies layout-guided streaming construction to speed up updates and limit serving interference. Extensive evaluation shows that ZeroGR accelerates the filtering and scoring pipeline by up to $9.9\times$ over representative baselines while reducing GPU index memory use and accelerating index reconstruction.

papers.title: Where Is the Truth When AI Agents Disagree? Dependence-Aware Belief Propagation for Unsupervised Truth Discovery (Extended Version)
papers.abstract: LLM agents often give conflicting answers to the same question, and many deployed agents are variants of one base model, so their errors are correlated. We study truth discovery among such agents: inferring the true answer and each agent's reliability without labels. Classical truth-discovery and crowdsourcing estimators reward an agreeing bloc and can fall below majority vote. We propose BP-TD, which adds per-agent decorrelation weights to mean-field variational inference on a one-coin Dawid-Skene model, so that agents sharing a base model count together as about one vote. Its first iteration is exactly a weighted vote; later iterations estimate agent reliability. With 13 local agents on MMLU, BP-TD beats majority vote without any labels (0.716 vs. 0.624 on 160 questions; 0.707 vs. 0.674 on 10,000) and ranks agents by their true accuracy, which classical estimators invert. The gain depends on the pool: over 2,852 sub-pools of four benchmarks, decorrelation helps when the largest correlated bloc is weaker than the other agents and hurts when it is the strongest, and we found no label-free statistic that tells the two cases apart. Labels change the picture quickly: with 20 labelled questions, selecting the single best agent is more accurate than every aggregator we tested on MMLU, ARC and TruthfulQA.

papers.title: Knowledge Graph Lakehouse: A Cloud-Native Architecture for Managing Enterprise Knowledge Graphs at Scale
papers.abstract: Modern data architectures for integrating heterogeneous data sources to discover actionable knowledge include the data warehouse, the data lake, and the data lakehouse, which combines the flexibility of the data lake with the structured data management capabilities of the data warehouse through metadata, indexes, and caching. Enterprise knowledge graphs (KGs) offer an alternative approach to such integration for the purposes of data analysis, but handling them at scale must address the Three Vs of big data: volume, velocity, and variety. Contextualized KGs (CKGs) meet part of that challenge by enriching facts with contextual information, yet many applications require only a context-specific subset of that knowledge. We propose the Knowledge Graph Lakehouse (KG Lakehouse), a cloud-native microservice architecture that adapts the data lakehouse paradigm for management of CKGs at scale. The KG Lakehouse indexes incoming source documents along configurable context dimensions and stores these documents in a data lake, from which application-specific CKGs are constructed on demand instead of maintaining a single, monolithic KG. We realize the proposed architecture as a proof of concept, with independently deployable services built from established cloud technology; context dimensions and format-specific document handling enter as configuration, leaving the architecture independent of the application domain. We evaluate the implemented system in experiments on a distributed cluster deployment.

papers.title: Correctness Firewalls for Synthesized Database Components
papers.abstract: For the first time in history, high-performance code is cheap. Today's coding agents can generate bespoke, instance-optimized data systems with excellent performance, and such agents will continue to improve as LLMs advance. But a purely agentic approach, even when validated with strong testing techniques, does not automatically inherit the correctness guarantees our community has spent decades building. We propose a middle ground between hand-crafted and agent-crafted systems: correctness firewalls, lightweight design patterns under which a synthesized component can affect a system's performance but never its results. Behind a correctness firewall, agents are free to synthesize fast components while the overall system remains correct. We present three case studies, each demonstrating a different type of firewall: cardinality estimation (advisory), searching sorted data (guarded), and data compression (certified). In early experiments, synthesized components search sorted data up to 3x faster than human-designed learned indexes and can compress text 1.5x smaller than Zstd. Drawing on these case studies, we outline a research agenda for how data management systems can exploit coding agents without giving up their hard-won correctness guarantees, from protecting synthesized code to measuring the cost of correctness.

papers.title: SSPE: Robust Sequential Staypoint Extraction in Degraded Trajectory Data
papers.abstract: Extracting semantically meaningful staypoints from raw trajectory streams is a foundational prerequisite for mobility analytics. However, real-world trajectory data is frequently degraded by severe spatial noise and protracted temporal dropouts. Classic threshold-based extraction methods, such as the widely adopted sliding-window algorithm, are highly sensitive to these anomalies, routinely fracturing continuous stationary episodes into disjointed fragments. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Sequential Staypoint Extraction (SSPE) algorithm. SSPE employs a resilient, state-driven architecture that replaces static spatial anchors with a dynamic centroid and introduces an $n$-step lookahead heuristic to structurally tolerate transient coordinate drift. Concurrently, it utilizes temporal bridging mechanisms to prevent artificial fragmentation during prolonged signal loss. Since optimal extraction parameters vary significantly across datasets, we further introduce a fully unsupervised, consensus-based parameter estimation framework. This framework derives baseline statistical scales directly from the raw trajectory data and identifies the optimal parameter configuration by maximizing structural agreement, thereby eliminating the reliance on annotated ground truth. We evaluate SSPE on the ExtraSensory dataset, a real-world mobility corpus with manually verified ground-truth staypoints, against the sliding-window implementation of Trackintel, one of the most widely adopted extraction baselines in the field. Empirical results demonstrate that SSPE achieves superior accuracy, yielding higher F1-scores while simultaneously improving computational efficiency over this standard.

papers.title: Modular and Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbors Search with Vectorium and kANNolo
papers.abstract: Approximate Nearest Neighbors (ANN) search over neural embeddings powers modern retrieval systems such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Embeddings come in three representations (dense, sparse and multi-vector), and efficient search combines an index structure, a similarity function and a quantization scheme. Existing libraries fix one combination, hard-code each one separately, or factor only one side of the problem, and none covers all three representations. We present Vectorium and kANNolo, two open-source Rust libraries that split this design space into a data-management layer and an indexing layer. Vectorium abstracts the vector, the distance function, the quantizer and the dataset independently, and provides 11 encoders, from 32-bit floats to sub-bit codes. On top of it, kANNolo implements Hierarchical Navigable Small-World (HNSW) graph and Inverted Vector File (IVF) indexes that are generic over representation, encoder and metric, and a two-stage index that composes any first-stage index with any rescoring dataset. Since every combination is specialized at compile time, this modularity adds no run-time overhead, and the resulting indexes reach state-of-the-art performance: our Product Quantization matches Faiss in accuracy at competitive speed, our RaBitQ and HNSW match or outperform their reference implementations, and our IVF outperforms Faiss. Against six dense and five sparse systems on seven public collections, our indexes give the best memory-throughput trade-off on dense data in 9 of 12 collection-accuracy pairs and perform well on out-of-distribution queries. On sparse data, the systems built on Vectorium lead on all three collections, with Seismic and SeismicWave the fastest and kANNolo's indexes the most compact.

papers.title: The Power of Bidegeneracy for Hypergraph Data Structures
papers.abstract: A hypergraph $H = (V,E)$ describes a set system over a vertex universe $V$. Hypergraphs are increasingly popular in network science, as they represent interactions between subsets of vertices. A natural challenge is to design a data structure for $H$ to quickly answer basic questions about it, e.g. how many neighbors a vertex $v$ has or whether a hyperedge contains a vertex subset $S$. Such questions are trivial for graphs, for which we simply inspect the adjacency list. The gold standard, from a data structures perspective, would be near-linear time preprocessing and query answering in (poly)logarithmic time. Since this is unlikely for arbitrary $H$, we ask for well-motivated hypergraph properties that can make such a goal possible. We introduce bidegeneracy, a measure of hypergraph sparsity that strictly generalizes many other measures, including bounded degree, bounded rank, and bounded $\infty$-degeneracy. We show that bounded bidegeneracy yields fast hypergraph data structures. For a large set of fundamental queries, including their listing and sampling versions, we obtain near-linear preprocessing and (poly)logarithmic query time. Moreover, direct reductions from assumptions like the Orthogonal Vectors Conjecture suggest that, without assumptions on the input, these structures require almost-quadratic preprocessing or almost-linear query time. We use bidegeneracy to compute a compressed representation of $H$ and perform careful reductions to stabbing and searching problems in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Our framework significantly extends the well-studied "partial matching" problem of finding database entries through wildcard search. It also uncovers an intriguing connection between hypergraph sparsity, compression, and the complexity of hypergraph primitives. We also find remarkably low bidegeneracy in hypergraph datasets from the literature, suggesting practical consequences.

papers.title: Extending the MM-AR Metamodeling Platform with Process Mining Capabilities
papers.abstract: Process mining derives process models from event data recorded by information systems, but its results are usually presented as two-dimensional visualizations that are separate from the environments in which enterprise models are created and maintained. Metamodeling platforms for extended reality (XR), such as MM-AR, allow users to define modeling languages and to display models in 2D and 3D, but they do not provide access to event data or mining algorithms so far. In this paper we therefore present a first proof-of-concept for showing how an XR-based metamodeling platform can be extended with process discovery capabilities without changes to the platform core through a separate Python service based on the open source PM4Py process mining library. We demonstrate the approach using three common discovery algorithms for obtaining Petri nets and BPMN models based on CSV or XES event logs. A technical evaluation using four public event logs shows that the element counts of the created model instances match those of the PM4Py models in all 16 configurations. The integration adds between about 8 and 53 seconds per run, and this overhead grows with the size of the discovered model rather than the size of the event log. Although the prototype does not yet use the third dimension to encode process information, it established the foundations for studying such approaches.

papers.title: Complexity of conjunctive regular path query homomorphisms
papers.abstract: A graph database is a digraph whose arcs are labeled with symbols from a fixed alphabet. A regular graph pattern (RGP) is a digraph whose arcs are labeled with regular expressions over the alphabet. RGPs model navigational queries for graph databases called \emph{conjunctive regular path queries} (CRPQs). A match of a CRPQ in the database is witnessed by a special navigational homomorphism of the corresponding RGP to the database, where vertices of the RGP are mapped by a function $f$ to the vertices of the database, and for each arc $uv$ of the RGP, we require the existence of a walk in the database from $f(u)$ to $f(v)$, such that the word corresponding to the sequence of labels of that walk belongs to the regular language labeling the arc $uv$. We extend this definition to one of navigational homomorphisms between two RGPs, modeling a homomorphism-based form of CRPQ containment. We study the complexity of deciding the existence of such a homomorphism between RGPs. We show that this problem, in the case where general walks are considered, can still be solved by an EXPSPACE algorithm (just like general CRPQ Containment, which is known to be EXPSPACE-complete). In the case of simple paths or trails, in fact the navigational homomorphism problem considered here becomes much more tractable, as it is PSPACE-complete. We also study the problem for restricted RGPs over a unary alphabet, that arise from some applications like XPath or SPARQL. For this case, homomorphism-based CRPQ containment is in NP. We prove that certain interesting cases are in fact polynomial-time solvable.

papers.title: How to Define the Quality of Data? A Feature-Based Literature Survey
papers.abstract: Data is generated in almost every digital interaction, and using it effectively requires high quality. But what exactly is data quality? The literature offers many, widely diverging answers. This article presents a systematic literature review that screened more than 8,700 records on data quality and identified 35 providing original, dimension-based definitions. Using feature-oriented domain analysis, a feature model of these heterogeneous definitions is derived and used to classify all identified publications. The classification reveals a heterogeneous landscape: despite an ISO standard and a few highly cited quasi-standards, no consensus exists on which quality dimensions to consider or how to define them. As definitions increasingly emerge for specific domains, contexts of use, and new types of data, the respective communities need to deliberately converge on how data quality is defined in their field.

papers.title: Teach Your DBMS to LIKE Strings: Fast and General Pattern Matching for Wildcard Joins and Filters
papers.abstract: Nowadays, modern applications do more than just store text -- they need to derive meaningful insights from it. To do that, they usually rely on wildcard queries with LIKE predicate to extract patterns. However, modern database management systems (DBMSs) handle these wildcard operations poorly, resorting to nested loops for joins and expensive interpreted evaluation for filters. To address the former, we propose a new join algorithm based on the Aho-Corasick algorithm, which significantly reduces the time complexity. For wildcard filtering, we leverage the code-generation infrastructure to improve performance: we generate specialized code for the LIKE predicate, eliminating the overhead of interpreting the pattern per tuple. Our experimental results show that the new wildcard join algorithm significantly outperforms both baseline DuckDB and Umbra, achieving speedups of up to 30.6x and 114.75x, respectively. The new wildcard filter approach likewise outperforms both baselines, achieving a speedup of 13.3x in a filter-focused stress benchmark. We believe these two techniques will play key roles for high-performance text analytics in modern query engines.

papers.title: FPT iff PTIME for Homomorphism Problems on Sparse-Incidence and Bounded-Independence Patterns
papers.abstract:
We show that fixed-parameter tractability and polynomial-time solvability coincide for homomorphism problems specified by classes of pattern hypergraphs of bounded incidence degeneracy or bounded primal independence number, assuming $FPT 
e W[1]$. In both cases, tractability is characterised by bounded fractional hypertree width. This generalises a result of Grohe [JACM 2007] that established such an FPT-PTIME collapse for bounded-arity structures. We build on the fractional balanced-separator framework and rounding theorem of Korchemna, Lokshtanov, Saurabh, Surianarayanan, and Xue [FOCS 2024] to prove near-linear bounds on fractional hypertree width ($fhw$) in terms of adaptive width ($adw$). Namely, for every hypergraph $H$ $$fhw(H)=O(\mu(H) adw(H)\log adw(H)), \quad fhw(H)=O(\log \alpha(H) adw(H)\log adw(H))$$ where $\mu(H)$ is the degeneracy of the incidence graph of $H$ and $\alpha(H)$ the independence number of the primal graph of $H$. As a consequence, we obtain a corresponding FPT-PTIME collapse for exact homomorphism decision and counting on every class in which either incidence degeneracy or independence number is bounded. This includes a number of natural classes such as pattern hypergraphs of bounded degree. Additionally, we observe that for every r.e. class of pattern hypergraphs, fixed-parameter tractability of the parameterised homomorphism problem implies quasipolynomial-time solvability of the corresponding unparameterised problem, assuming $FPT 
e W[1]$. Our results rely on the characterisation of fixed-parameter tractable decision of homomorphism problems in terms of submodular width of Marx [JACM 2013], conditional on ETH. In light of the very recent potential refutation of the ETH, we show that the characterisation of Marx holds also under the assumption that $FPT 
e W[1]$.

papers.title: Why Tabular Foundation Models Excel on Relational Data They Have Never Seen
papers.abstract: Given a relational database (RDB) storing heterogeneous tabular information, how can we predict missing (or future) values in some target column of interest? As candidate targets are numerous in enterprise settings, it is preferable to avoid learning a new model from scratch each time there is a new prediction task. Frozen foundation models (FMs) based on in-context learning (ICL) and RDB-specific pre-training provide a viable solution, but the ideal design still remains largely unresolved. Perhaps unexpectedly, preliminary evidence has recently shown that existing single-table FMs (aka TFMs), when combined with suitable parameter-free relational encoders, can be quite competitive in practice despite zero exposure to RDB pre-training or relational data of any kind. In this work we first empirically confirm this phenomenon with a more diverse array of experiments. We then turn to our main contribution, namely, surfacing multiple complementary explanations for why TFMs behave so effectively. These explanations ultimately hinge on innate synergies whereby parameter-free encoders map relational effects to fixed-length embeddings that loosely mimic distributions for which TFMs were originally designed; in so doing, desirable single-table properties transfer to relational settings (e.g., convergent posterior predictive distributions). Collectively, our analysis forges new pathways for improving RDB FMs, particularly when we prioritize interpretability and inevitable integration within agentic systems.
